summary: Describes a lighter form of IP-in-IP tunneling that adds less overhead than the usual method of adding a second full IP header. It reuses information from the original header to save space.

plainLanguage.summary: To send a datagram through a tunnel, the usual way is to wrap it in a second complete IP header, which repeats information the first header already has. This document defines a smaller way: a short forwarding header of 8 or 12 bytes that keeps only what the receiver needs to put the datagram back together.

questions: what is minimal encapsulation in ip
how does minimal encapsulation differ from ip in ip
how big is the minimal forwarding header
subtitle: A lighter IP tunnel that inserts a small forwarding header instead of wrapping a whole second IP header.

tldr.problem: Conventional IP-in-IP encapsulation adds a complete second IP header to every datagram, duplicating fields the original header already carries and wasting space on every packet.
tldr.mechanism: The document inserts a minimal forwarding header of 8 or 12 octets after the modified IP header instead. It keeps only the original destination address and, optionally, the original source address, and marks the datagram with IP protocol number 55.
tldr.outcome: The tunnel costs 8 or 12 octets of overhead instead of a whole extra header, at the price of not carrying fragmentation information, so it cannot be used on an already fragmented datagram.

today: RFC 2004 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The document leaves routing-loop handling and ICMP behaviour to RFC 2003 and points at RFC 2002 for the Mobile IP scheme that motivated it.

sections.title: What Minimal Encapsulation Does
sections.content:
This document specifies a method by which an IP datagram may be encapsulated, carried as payload, within an IP datagram, with less overhead than conventional IP encapsulation, which adds a second IP header to each encapsulated datagram. Encapsulation is suggested as a means to alter the normal IP routing for datagrams, by delivering them to an intermediate destination that would otherwise not be selected by the network part of the IP Destination Address field in the original IP header.

The process of encapsulating and decapsulating a datagram is frequently called tunneling the datagram. The encapsulator and decapsulator are the endpoints of the tunnel: the encapsulator node is the entry point and the decapsulator node is the exit point.

The document is short and leaves the details of the surrounding mechanism to other documents. It specifies the header format and the rules for changing and restoring the IP header, and it defers routing-loop handling and ICMP behaviour to RFC 2003.
sections.plainLanguage: Tunneling means wrapping a datagram so that it travels to a different place than its address would normally send it. This document describes a way of doing that with less added weight than the usual one.

sections.title: Why a Lighter Tunnel
sections.content:
The Mobile IP working group has specified the use of encapsulation as a way to deliver packets from a mobile node's home network to an agent that can deliver datagrams locally by conventional means to the mobile node at its current location away from home. The use of encapsulation may also be indicated whenever the source, or an intermediate router, of an IP datagram must influence the route by which the datagram is delivered to its ultimate destination.

Other possible applications of encapsulation include multicasting, preferential billing, choice of routes with selected security attributes, and general policy routing.

Using IP headers to encapsulate IP datagrams requires the unnecessary duplication of several fields within the inner IP header. It is possible to save some additional space by specifying a new encapsulation mechanism that eliminates the duplication. The scheme here comes from the Mobile IP Working Group, in earlier Internet-Drafts, and is similar to the one defined in RFC 2002 and to the scheme described by Johnson in the literature.
sections.plainLanguage: Mobile IP was the first reason this was written. The bigger reason is simple: a second full header repeats addresses and other fields that the first header already has, and that costs bytes on every single packet.

sections.title: How the Encapsulation Works
sections.content:
A minimal forwarding header is defined for datagrams that are not fragmented prior to encapsulation. Use of this encapsulating method is optional. Minimal encapsulation MUST NOT be used when an original datagram is already fragmented, since there is no room in the minimal forwarding header to store fragmentation information.

To encapsulate an IP datagram, the minimal forwarding header is inserted into the datagram. The IP header of the original datagram is modified, the minimal forwarding header is inserted after the IP header, and the unmodified IP payload of the original datagram follows, for example the transport header and transport data. No additional IP header is added to the datagram.

The original IP header is modified as follows. The Protocol field is replaced by protocol number 55, for the minimal encapsulation protocol. The Destination Address field is replaced by the IP address of the exit point of the tunnel. If the encapsulator is not the original source of the datagram, the Source Address field is replaced by the IP address of the encapsulator. The Total Length field is incremented by the size of the minimal forwarding header, which is either 12 or 8 octets depending on whether the Original Source Address Present bit is set. The Header Checksum field is recomputed or updated to account for the changes.

Unlike IP-in-IP encapsulation, the Time to Live field is not modified during encapsulation. If the encapsulator is forwarding the datagram, it decrements the TTL as a result of normal IP forwarding. Because the original TTL remains in the header after encapsulation, hops taken by the datagram within the tunnel are visible, for example to traceroute.

When decapsulating, the fields in the minimal forwarding header are restored to the IP header and the forwarding header is removed from the datagram. The Total Length field is decremented by the size of the minimal forwarding header removed, and the Header Checksum is recomputed or updated.

The encapsulator may use existing IP mechanisms appropriate for delivery of the encapsulated payload to the tunnel exit point. Use of IP options is allowed, and use of fragmentation is allowed unless the Don't Fragment bit is set in the IP header. That restriction on fragmentation is required so that nodes employing Path MTU Discovery can obtain the information they seek.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender rewrites the outer header so the datagram goes to the tunnel exit, then slips in a short header that keeps the original address. On arrival the exit point puts everything back the way it was and removes the short header. The time-to-live counter is not reset, so a traceroute still sees the hops inside the tunnel.

sections.title: The Minimal Forwarding Header
sections.content:
The minimal forwarding header is 8 octets, or 12 octets when the original source address is carried. It is transmitted from left to right in the format the document draws as a bit diagram.

The Protocol field is 8 bits and is copied from the Protocol field in the original IP header. The Original Source Address Present bit, the S bit, follows it. When the S bit is 0 the Original Source Address field is not present and the header is 8 octets long. When the S bit is 1 the field is present and the header is 12 octets long. The reserved field is sent as zero and ignored on reception.

The Header Checksum is 16 bits and is the 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of all 16-bit words in the minimal forwarding header. For computing it the checksum field's own value is 0. The IP header and the IP payload that follow the minimal forwarding header are not included in this checksum computation.

The Original Destination Address is 32 bits and is copied from the Destination Address field in the original IP header. The Original Source Address is 32 bits and is copied from the Source Address field in the original IP header. It is present only when the S bit is set.
sections.plainLanguage: The short header holds the original protocol number, the original destination address and, if you want the original sender recorded too, the original source address. A checksum over those fields lets the receiver notice damage.

sections.title: Routing Failures and ICMP
sections.content:
The use of any encapsulation method for routing purposes brings with it increased susceptibility to routing loops. To cut down the danger, a router should follow the same procedures outlined in RFC 2003.

ICMP messages are to be handled as specified in RFC 2003, including the maintenance of tunnel soft state.
sections.plainLanguage: Routing a datagram by a detour raises the chance of a loop, so the document points at the rules in RFC 2003 for breaking one. Error messages inside the tunnel are handled the same way, including the soft state that tracks a tunnel.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Security considerations are not addressed in this document, but are generally similar to those outlined in RFC 2003.
sections.plainLanguage: The document does not discuss security. It says the same considerations as RFC 2003 apply, and points readers there.

fields.name: Protocol
fields.desc: Copied from the Protocol field in the original IP header.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: Original Source Address Present. 0 means the source address is absent and the header is 8 octets; 1 means it is present and the header is 12 octets.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Sent as zero; ignored on reception.

fields.name: Header Checksum
fields.desc: The 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of all 16-bit words in the minimal forwarding header, with the checksum field taken as 0.

fields.name: Original Destination Address
fields.desc: Copied from the Destination Address field in the original IP header.

fields.name: Original Source Address
fields.desc: Copied from the Source Address field in the original IP header. Present only if the S bit is set.

left.title: IP-in-IP
left.desc: Adds a second complete IP header, duplicating fields the original header already carries.

right.title: Minimal encapsulation
right.desc: Adds a forwarding header of 8 or 12 octets holding the original protocol number and destination address, and optionally the original source address.

messages.label: Modified IP header plus minimal forwarding header
messages.note: Protocol 55, destination address set to the exit point.

messages.label: IP datagram
messages.note: Forwarding header removed and the original fields restored.
